title: 🌿 Ecosystem Explorer
description: Welcome to the Ecosystem Explorer! You are a Grade 6 student joining the school's new Ecology Club. Over 14 weeks, you will study living ecosystems — from tiny decomposers to apex predators. Build food chains, track energy flow, investigate habitats, and protect biodiversity. When invasive species and pollution threaten your study sites, it is up to you and your team to find solutions. Can you become the Ecosystem Champion by Conservation Day?
subject: science
how_to_play: You are a Grade 6 student exploring ecosystems and ecology over a 14-week field study program.
Each week presents an ecology challenge with choices that affect your knowledge, field skills, and ecosystem health.
Watch your dashboard — your Study Zones (Forest, Pond, Soil, Grassland, Urban Garden) are interconnected.
NPCs like Dr. Leaf (teacher), Fern (nature guide), Anika, and Sam react to your decisions.
Random events like animal sightings and weather changes will test your adaptability.
Keep Ecosystem Health high — if biodiversity drops too low, the ecosystem collapses!
learning_objectives: Understand the roles of producers, consumers, and decomposers in an ecosystem
Build and interpret food chains and food webs
Compare different habitats and the organisms adapted to each
Analyze predator-prey relationships and population dynamics
Evaluate human impact on ecosystems and biodiversity
Design and propose conservation strategies for local ecosystems
cultural_context: School ecology field study, outdoor STEM learning, environmental stewardship

behaviors.message: I am worried about the ecosystem health readings. When biodiversity drops this low, entire food chains can collapse. We need to focus on conservation immediately.
You seem to be struggling with some ecology concepts. That is okay — nature is complex! Come to my office hours and we will review food chains and habitats together.
Outstanding work! Your ecology knowledge and conservation efforts are making a real difference. I am nominating you for the Junior Ecologist Award!
Your species catalog is remarkable! The detail and accuracy of your observations rival university-level field work. I want to submit your data to the regional biodiversity database!
I can feel the ecosystem struggling. Fewer birds singing, fewer insects buzzing. When biodiversity drops, the whole web of life weakens. We need to act now!
Our field equipment is in rough shape. Binoculars are foggy, sample jars are cracked. We cannot do good science with broken tools. Time for a maintenance day!
Listen to that! The frogs are singing, butterflies are everywhere, and I just spotted fresh deer tracks. This ecosystem is thriving thanks to your care!
You move through the forest like a real naturalist now — quiet, observant, respectful. Your field skills are impressive. Keep it up!
We are actually making a difference! The butterfly garden is attracting new species and the bird boxes have nests! What if we start a nature blog to share our progress?
Hey, ecology is a team sport! We cannot study an entire ecosystem alone. Can we please coordinate better instead of everyone wandering off on their own?
Our species catalog is growing so fast! I never knew there were so many types of beetles in the school garden. We are becoming real field biologists!
This does not look good. The pond is murky, there are barely any insects, and the soil smells wrong. I think we are losing the ecosystem. What should we do?
Our data collection methods are solid now. I have been graphing population trends and the patterns are fascinating. This is real ecological research!
We are collecting data all wrong. Without proper sampling techniques, our observations are unreliable. Science needs rigorous methods, not just wandering around looking at things.

I cross-referenced our species catalog with the regional database and found something interesting. Two of the species we recorded have not been seen in this area for 10 years! That is a sign of improving habitat!
Our team dynamics are excellent. Everyone knows their role — Anika documents, I analyze, and you coordinate. This is what real scientific collaboration looks like!

rounds.round_title: Week 1: Welcome to the Ecology Club
rounds.situation: It is your first day in the Ecology Club! Dr. Leaf gathers everyone near the school garden and says: 'An ecosystem is a community of living things interacting with their environment. This semester, we will explore the ecosystems right here on our school grounds — the forest patch, the pond, the garden, and the grassland.' How do you want to begin?
rounds.goal: Choose how to begin your ecology exploration.
rounds.coaching_moment: Delayed gratification: Learning to observe carefully before acting is the most important skill in ecology. Patient scientists see things others miss.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why do scientists spend time observing before they start experimenting?
rounds.image_prompt: Grade 6 students gathering outdoors near a school garden with trees and a small pond, teacher pointing at nature, excited faces, field notebooks and binoculars visible

choices.label: A. An ecosystem is another name for a habitat, meaning the place where animals live
choices.learning_concept: Ecosystem Definition — Biotic and Abiotic Factors
choices.feedback: Not exactly! 💡 A habitat and an ecosystem are different things. A habitat is just the physical place where an organism lives (like a pond or forest). An ecosystem is bigger — it includes the habitat PLUS all the living organisms AND their interactions with each other and with non-living things. Think of habitat as the 'address' and ecosystem as the whole 'neighborhood community'!

skill_explanation.resilience: Facing challenges head-on strengthens your resilience over time.

choices.label: B. An ecosystem is just the collection of all animals living in one place
choices.learning_concept: Ecosystem Definition — Biotic and Abiotic Factors
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 An ecosystem includes much more than just animals. It includes ALL living things (plants, fungi, bacteria too!) AND non-living things like water, rocks, sunlight, and air. The word 'eco' comes from the Greek word for 'home' — an ecosystem is the complete home, not just some of the residents!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Being open to new information and changing course builds adaptability.

choices.label: C. An ecosystem only includes the plants and trees in a forest
choices.learning_concept: Ecosystem Definition — Biotic and Abiotic Factors
choices.feedback: Not right! 💡 An ecosystem is not limited to plants or forests. It includes ALL living things (plants, animals, fungi, microorganisms) plus ALL non-living things (water, air, sunlight, minerals, temperature). Ecosystems can be a forest, a pond, a desert, or even a rotting log! Every ecosystem has both biotic (living) and abiotic (non-living) components.

skill_explanation.empathy: Understanding the impact on people around you shows care for others.

choices.label: D. An ecosystem includes all the living organisms AND non-living things (like water, sunlight, soil) in an area, interacting together
choices.learning_concept: Ecosystem Definition — Biotic and Abiotic Factors
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ An ecosystem is made up of two parts: biotic factors (living things like plants, animals, fungi, and bacteria) and abiotic factors (non-living things like water, sunlight, temperature, and soil). Both parts work together — for example, plants need sunlight (abiotic) to grow, and animals need plants (biotic) to eat!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

rounds.situation: Dr. Leaf brings the class to the garden and asks: 'Who makes their own food, and who has to eat someone else?' She introduces producers (plants that make food from sunlight), primary consumers (herbivores that eat plants), and secondary consumers (carnivores that eat herbivores). Your task: identify examples of each in the school ecosystem.
rounds.goal: Identify and classify organisms as producers, primary consumers, or secondary consumers.
rounds.coaching_moment: Strategic thinking: Understanding who eats whom is the key to understanding how energy flows through an ecosystem. Every organism has a role.
rounds.reflection_prompt: If all the producers (plants) in an ecosystem disappeared, what would happen to the consumers? Why?
rounds.image_prompt: School garden with visible food chain elements — plants, caterpillars eating leaves, a bird watching from a branch, student taking notes with a magnifying glass

choices.label: A. Consumers are only the animals that eat plants; animals that eat other animals are called predators, not consumers
choices.feedback: Close but not accurate! 💡 ALL animals that eat other organisms are consumers — whether they eat plants or other animals. Plant-eaters are primary consumers (herbivores), meat-eaters are secondary consumers (carnivores), and animals that eat both are omnivores. 'Predator' describes a behavior, but in the food chain, they are all classified as consumers!

skill_explanation.empathy: Listening to different viewpoints strengthens your empathy skills.

choices.label: B. Decomposers are the largest animals in an ecosystem because they eat everything
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Decomposers are actually some of the smallest organisms — bacteria, fungi, and earthworms. They do not hunt or eat living things. Instead, they break down dead plants and animals into simple nutrients that go back into the soil. Without decomposers, dead material would pile up everywhere and plants would run out of nutrients!

skill_explanation.resilience: Pushing through difficulty builds mental strength.

choices.label: C. Producers are organisms like green plants that make their own food using sunlight, while consumers are organisms that eat other organisms for energy
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Producers (like green plants and algae) use photosynthesis to convert sunlight into food energy. Consumers cannot make their own food — they must eat other organisms. Primary consumers (herbivores) eat producers, secondary consumers (carnivores) eat herbivores, and decomposers (like fungi and bacteria) break down dead material, recycling nutrients back into the soil!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.label: D. Any animal that eats a lot of food is called a producer because it produces energy
choices.feedback: That is a common mix-up! 💡 In ecology, 'producer' does not mean producing a lot of energy — it means MAKING food from scratch. Only organisms with chlorophyll (like green plants and algae) can do this through photosynthesis. Animals are always consumers because they must eat other organisms. They consume food; they do not produce it from sunlight!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Pivoting your strategy when needed is a sign of adaptive thinking.

rounds.situation: Dr. Leaf draws an arrow on the whiteboard: Grass → Rabbit → Fox. 'This is a food chain — it shows how energy moves from one organism to another. The arrow means is eaten by. Today, you will build food chains from the organisms you identified last week. But remember — every food chain starts with a producer!'
rounds.goal: Build accurate food chains from your field observations and understand energy transfer.
rounds.coaching_moment: Strategic thinking: Food chains show the flow of energy. Understanding these connections helps you predict what happens when one link is removed.
rounds.reflection_prompt: What would happen to foxes if all the rabbits in a food chain suddenly disappeared?
rounds.image_prompt: Whiteboard showing food chain diagram with arrows between organisms, student drawing additional food chains, colorful cards with animal pictures on desk

choices.label: A. A food chain starts with the biggest, strongest animal at the top because it has the most energy
choices.learning_concept: Food Chain Structure and Energy Flow
choices.feedback: Actually the opposite is true! 💡 Food chains always start with producers (plants) at the bottom, not predators at the top. The top predators actually have the LEAST total energy available to them. At each step in the food chain, about 90% of energy is lost as heat. So grass has far more total energy than the eagle that sits at the top!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Responding to unexpected situations with creativity shows adaptability.

choices.label: B. A food chain can start with any animal, like a tiger, because tigers are powerful enough to begin the chain
choices.learning_concept: Food Chain Structure and Energy Flow
choices.feedback: Not correct! 💡 A food chain MUST start with a producer — an organism that makes its own food through photosynthesis (like plants or algae). Tigers are top consumers; they receive energy that originally came from plants. Without producers at the start, there would be no energy entering the food chain for any animal to use!

skill_explanation.empathy: Valuing others' experiences alongside your own shows empathetic thinking.

choices.label: C. The arrows in a food chain point from the eater to the food it eats, showing what eats what
choices.learning_concept: Food Chain Structure and Energy Flow
choices.feedback: Watch the arrow direction! 💡 The arrows in a food chain actually point FROM the organism being eaten TO the organism eating it. This is because arrows show the direction of ENERGY FLOW, not 'who eats whom.' So: Grass → Rabbit → Fox means energy flows from grass to rabbit to fox. The arrow follows the energy, not the appetite!

skill_explanation.resilience: Choosing to persist when things get hard develops resilience.

choices.label: D. A food chain always starts with a producer (like grass) and shows the flow of energy in one straight path from organism to organism
choices.learning_concept: Food Chain Structure and Energy Flow
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ A food chain is a simple, linear path showing how energy flows from one organism to the next. It always starts with a producer (like grass or algae), then goes to a primary consumer (like a grasshopper), then a secondary consumer (like a frog), and so on. The arrows in a food chain point in the direction energy flows — from the eaten to the eater!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

rounds.situation: Dr. Leaf connects all the food chains on the board, and suddenly the simple lines become a tangled web. 'In reality, most organisms eat MORE than one thing and are eaten by MORE than one predator,' she explains. 'A food web shows ALL the feeding relationships in an ecosystem. It is much more complex — and much more realistic.' Sam is excited about the complexity, while Anika wonders how to draw it all.
rounds.goal: Build a food web by connecting multiple food chains and understand the web's complexity.
rounds.coaching_moment: Adaptability: Real ecosystems are messy webs of connections, not neat chains. Learning to see complexity without being overwhelmed is a superpower.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why is a food web more realistic than a single food chain? Why does this complexity actually make ecosystems stronger?
rounds.image_prompt: Complex food web diagram on a large poster with many organisms connected by arrows, students pointing at connections, colorful and detailed, classroom setting

choices.label: A. A food web is just a bigger food chain with more animals lined up in a single row
choices.learning_concept: Food Webs and Interconnected Feeding Relationships
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 A food web is not just a longer food chain. A food chain is a single straight line (Grass → Rabbit → Fox). A food web is a NETWORK with many branching connections. One organism can be part of several food chains at the same time. For example, a mouse might be eaten by a snake, an owl, AND a fox — creating multiple connected pathways!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Flexibility in your thinking helps you handle change effectively.

choices.label: B. Removing one species from a food web does not matter because other animals will simply eat something else
choices.learning_concept: Food Webs and Interconnected Feeding Relationships
choices.feedback: That is a dangerous assumption! 💡 Removing one species from a food web can cause a 'cascade effect' that disrupts many other species. For example, when wolves were removed from Yellowstone, deer overgrazed, killing trees, which caused riverbanks to erode! Some species are 'keystone species' — their removal collapses the entire web.

skill_explanation.resilience: Learning from setbacks rather than giving up shows resilience.

choices.label: C. A food web is made up of many interconnected food chains, showing that most organisms eat more than one type of food
choices.learning_concept: Food Webs and Interconnected Feeding Relationships
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ A food web is a network of many food chains that overlap and connect. In reality, most animals eat more than one thing — a bird might eat insects, seeds, AND worms. Food webs show these complex relationships. This is why removing one species can affect many others in the ecosystem, like pulling one thread in a spider's web!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: D. Food webs only exist in forests; simple ecosystems like ponds just have food chains
choices.learning_concept: Food Webs and Interconnected Feeding Relationships
choices.feedback: Not true! 💡 Food webs exist in EVERY ecosystem — forests, ponds, deserts, oceans, and even soil! A pond has a complex food web: algae are eaten by tadpoles and water fleas, which are eaten by dragonfly larvae and small fish, which are eaten by larger fish and frogs. Every ecosystem with multiple species has a food web, not just a single chain!

skill_explanation.empathy: Considering how others feel shows emotional intelligence.

rounds.situation: Dr. Leaf takes the class on a tour of all four study zones and asks: 'Why do different organisms live in different places? A frog does not live in a desert, and a cactus does not grow in a pond. Every organism has a habitat — the place where it lives — and a niche — the specific role it plays.' She assigns each team a different habitat to study in depth.
rounds.goal: Compare different habitats and understand why organisms are found where they are.
rounds.coaching_moment: Ethical reasoning: Every habitat has value, even ones that seem unpleasant like swamps or dark soil. Respecting all environments is the mark of a true ecologist.
rounds.reflection_prompt: What is the difference between a habitat and a niche? Give an example of each.
rounds.image_prompt: Split image showing four different habitats side by side — forest, pond, grassland, and garden — each with distinct organisms, students studying each one

choices.label: A. A niche and a habitat mean the same thing — they both describe where an animal lives
choices.feedback: They are actually different! 💡 A habitat is the physical place (like a pond, forest, or desert). A niche is much more — it is the organism's complete 'lifestyle': what it eats, what eats it, when it sleeps, how it reproduces, and how it interacts with other species. Two species can share a habitat but NEVER the exact same niche for long!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Adjusting your approach when conditions change shows flexibility.

choices.label: B. Only animals have niches; plants do not have niches because they cannot move around
choices.feedback: Plants have niches too! 💡 Even though plants cannot move, they each have a unique ecological niche. A tall tree's niche includes capturing sunlight above the canopy, while a fern's niche is growing in the shady understory. Plants also have niches based on which pollinators they attract, what soil they need, and when they flower. Every living thing has a niche!

skill_explanation.resilience: Staying focused under pressure builds your ability to bounce back.

choices.label: C. The biggest, strongest animal always gets the best habitat, and smaller animals take whatever is left
choices.feedback: Nature does not work like that! 💡 Habitats are not 'claimed' by the strongest. Different organisms are ADAPTED to different habitats. A polar bear is powerful but would struggle in a desert, while a tiny cactus thrives there. Each organism is suited to its own habitat through adaptations built up over millions of years of evolution. There is no 'best' habitat — just the right fit!

skill_explanation.empathy: Taking others' perspectives into account builds empathy.

choices.label: D. A habitat is the physical place where an organism lives, while a niche is the organism's specific role — what it eats, when it is active, and how it interacts with others
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Think of it this way: a habitat is your ADDRESS (where you live), while a niche is your JOB (what you do). Two birds might share the same forest habitat but have different niches — one eats insects from tree bark while the other catches insects in mid-air. This is called 'niche partitioning' and it allows many species to coexist!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

rounds.situation: Dr. Leaf asks a fascinating question: 'How did the giraffe get its long neck? Why can an owl see in the dark? How do desert plants survive with almost no water?' This week is all about adaptations — the special features that help organisms survive in their specific habitats. Anika is fascinated by camouflage, while Sam wants to study how plants compete for sunlight.
rounds.goal: Understand structural, behavioral, and physiological adaptations and why they matter.
rounds.coaching_moment: Resilience: Adaptations are nature's way of solving problems. Every challenge creates an opportunity for creative solutions — in ecosystems and in life.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Humans adapt to different environments too (clothing, houses, technology). How are human adaptations similar to and different from animal adaptations?
rounds.image_prompt: Collage showing amazing animal adaptations — chameleon changing color, owl's eyes in darkness, cactus with thick stem, student sketching adaptations in notebook

choices.label: A. An animal can decide to adapt its body during its own lifetime — like a rabbit choosing to grow thicker fur when winter comes
choices.feedback: This is a very common misconception! 💡 Animals cannot choose or decide to adapt. Adaptations are genetic changes that happen over MANY generations through natural selection. A rabbit that grows thicker winter fur has that ability because of genes it inherited — it did not 'decide' to grow fur. Its ancestors with thicker fur survived better and passed on those genes!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Being open to new information and changing course builds adaptability.

choices.label: B. All adaptations are physical features you can see, like claws, wings, or fur color
choices.feedback: There are many types of adaptations! 💡 Structural adaptations are physical (claws, thick fur, webbed feet). But there are also behavioral adaptations (birds migrating south for winter, bears hibernating) and physiological adaptations (camels storing fat in humps, some fish making antifreeze proteins). Adaptations can be things you see, do, or that happen inside the body!

skill_explanation.empathy: Understanding the impact on people around you shows care for others.

choices.label: C. Camouflage is not a real adaptation — animals just happen to look like their surroundings by accident
choices.feedback: Camouflage is a brilliant adaptation! 💡 Over many generations, animals that blended into their backgrounds were less likely to be eaten by predators, so they survived longer and had more babies. Their 'blending-in' genes were passed on. This is why leaf insects look exactly like leaves and arctic hares turn white in winter — natural selection shaped these amazing disguises!

skill_explanation.resilience: Facing challenges head-on strengthens your resilience over time.

choices.label: D. Adaptations are traits that develop over many generations through natural selection, helping a species survive better in its environment
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Adaptations happen over many generations, not in one lifetime. When some individuals have a trait that helps them survive better (like thicker fur in cold places), they are more likely to reproduce and pass that trait to offspring. Over thousands of years, the whole population changes. This is natural selection — nature 'selects' the best-suited traits!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

rounds.situation: EMERGENCY! During routine monitoring, Fern discovers a rapidly spreading invasive water hyacinth choking the school pond. The floating plants block sunlight, use up oxygen, and are killing native fish and frogs. Dr. Leaf is alarmed: 'This is a real ecological crisis. Invasive species can destroy entire ecosystems. How we respond will determine if our pond survives.' The biodiversity index is dropping fast!
rounds.goal: Respond to an invasive species crisis and develop a management strategy.
rounds.coaching_moment: Resilience: Ecological crises test your problem-solving under pressure. The best response combines quick action with long-term planning.
rounds.reflection_prompt: What makes a species 'invasive'? Why are invasive species one of the biggest threats to biodiversity worldwide?
rounds.image_prompt: School pond covered with thick green water hyacinth, dead fish visible, worried students and teacher examining the situation, someone pulling out plants, murky water

choices.label: A. Parasitism is when two species compete for the same food, like two birds eating the same berries
choices.feedback: That describes competition, not parasitism! 💡 Parasitism is when one organism (the parasite) lives on or inside another organism (the host) and takes nutrients from it, causing harm. Mosquitoes drinking blood, mistletoe stealing water from trees, and tapeworms in intestines are all parasites. Two birds eating the same berries is called interspecific competition — a different type of interaction!

skill_explanation.resilience: Pushing through difficulty builds mental strength.

choices.label: B. Symbiosis only means a helpful relationship where both species always benefit equally
choices.feedback: Not all symbiosis is helpful! 💡 Symbiosis just means 'living together closely.' It includes three types: mutualism (both benefit), commensalism (only one benefits, the other is unaffected), and parasitism (one benefits while HARMING the other). A tapeworm living inside someone's intestines is symbiosis too — harmful parasitism. Do not let the word 'together' fool you into thinking it is always friendly!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Pivoting your strategy when needed is a sign of adaptive thinking.

choices.label: C. Symbiosis is a close, long-term relationship between two different species — it can be mutualism (both benefit), commensalism (one benefits, other unaffected), or parasitism (one benefits, other harmed)
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Symbiosis means 'living together.' In mutualism, both species win — like bees getting nectar while pollinating flowers. In commensalism, one benefits and the other is not affected — like a bird nesting in a tree. In parasitism, one organism (the parasite) benefits while harming the other (the host) — like a tick feeding on a dog's blood!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.label: D. Commensalism is when one animal eats another animal, like a lion eating a zebra
choices.feedback: That is predation, not commensalism! 💡 Commensalism is when one species benefits and the other is neither helped nor harmed. For example, remora fish attach to sharks for free transportation and leftover food scraps, while the shark is not affected at all. A lion eating a zebra is predation — a predator-prey relationship, which is very different from commensalism!

skill_explanation.empathy: Listening to different viewpoints strengthens your empathy skills.

rounds.round_title: Week 8: The Hidden World of Decomposers
rounds.situation: After the invasive species crisis, Dr. Leaf turns attention to the least glamorous but most essential organisms in any ecosystem — decomposers. 'Without fungi, bacteria, and detritivores, dead matter would pile up forever and nutrients would be locked away,' she says. 'Decomposers complete the cycle of life.' She hands out magnifying glasses and leads the class to the soil study zone.
rounds.goal: Explore decomposers and understand their vital role in nutrient recycling.
rounds.coaching_moment: Empathy: The most important players in an ecosystem are often the ones nobody notices. Learning to appreciate invisible contributions is wisdom — in ecology and in life.
rounds.reflection_prompt: How is the role of decomposers similar to the role of people who clean up and maintain things in your school or community?
rounds.image_prompt: Students examining leaf litter and soil with magnifying glasses, visible mushrooms and worms, decomposing log with fungi, rich dark soil, science lab background

choices.label: A. Predators always keep the prey population at exactly the same number, so it never changes
choices.feedback: Populations are never perfectly stable! 💡 Predator and prey populations actually rise and fall in a CYCLE. When prey are abundant, predators thrive and multiply. But more predators means more hunting, which reduces prey. Then predators run low on food and decline, allowing prey to bounce back. This up-and-down pattern is one of ecology's most fascinating discoveries!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Responding to unexpected situations with creativity shows adaptability.

choices.label: B. Predators only eat sick animals, so they have no real effect on the total prey population size
choices.feedback: Predators have a big effect! 💡 While predators do sometimes catch weak or sick prey (which is helpful), they catch healthy prey too. Predators significantly control prey population sizes. When predator populations grow, prey numbers drop noticeably. Studies of wolves, lions, and sharks all show that predators are major regulators of prey populations, not just cleaners of the sick!

skill_explanation.resilience: Choosing to persist when things get hard develops resilience.

choices.label: C. When the prey population increases, predator numbers increase too (more food), but then prey decreases (more hunting), causing predator numbers to drop — creating a repeating cycle
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Predator and prey populations follow a cycle: more prey → more food for predators → predator population grows → more hunting reduces prey → less food for predators → predator population drops → prey recovers → cycle repeats! The classic example is lynx and snowshoe hares in Canada, where their populations rise and fall in a regular pattern.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: D. If all predators were removed from an ecosystem, the prey animals would be healthier and the ecosystem would thrive
choices.feedback: Removing predators actually harms ecosystems! 💡 Without predators, prey populations explode and overgraze vegetation, destroying habitats for other species. Deer without wolves in parts of the USA ate so many plants that songbirds lost nesting sites and riverbanks eroded. Predators keep ecosystems balanced by controlling prey numbers — they are essential, not harmful!

skill_explanation.ethical_reasoning: Weighing the ethical implications shows principled reasoning.

rounds.situation: Dr. Leaf introduces the concept of energy pyramids: 'Only about 10% of energy passes from one trophic level to the next. That means if grass captures 10,000 units of energy from the sun, rabbits get only 1,000, and foxes get only 100!' Sam is fascinated by the math, and Anika realizes why there are always fewer predators than prey.
rounds.goal: Understand energy pyramids and why energy decreases at each trophic level.
rounds.coaching_moment: Strategic thinking: The 10% rule explains why ecosystems are shaped like pyramids. Understanding energy flow helps you predict population sizes and ecosystem limits.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why does eating plants directly give you more energy than eating animals that ate those plants?
rounds.image_prompt: Energy pyramid diagram on poster board — wide base of producers, narrower herbivore layer, small predator layer at top, arrows showing energy loss, student presenting

choices.label: A. Only about 10% of the energy at one level of a food chain is passed to the next level — the rest is used by the organism for life processes and lost as heat
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ This is called the 10% Rule. When a rabbit eats grass, it uses about 90% of the energy for moving, growing, body heat, and digestion. Only about 10% is stored in its body as new tissue. When a fox eats the rabbit, it only gets that 10%. This is why energy pyramids are wide at the bottom (lots of plants) and narrow at the top (few top predators)!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: B. 100% of energy passes from one level to the next because energy cannot be created or destroyed
choices.feedback: Good thinking about energy conservation, but it does not work that way in food chains! 💡 While energy IS conserved overall (law of conservation of energy), organisms USE most of the energy they consume for body processes — movement, growth, warmth, and digestion. This energy is released as heat into the environment. Only about 10% gets stored as body mass for the next consumer!

skill_explanation.resilience: Learning from setbacks rather than giving up shows resilience.

choices.label: C. Energy increases at each level of the food chain because larger animals are more powerful and have more energy
choices.feedback: It is actually the opposite! 💡 Even though top predators are big and powerful individually, the TOTAL energy available at each level DECREASES going up the food chain. If plants capture 10,000 units of energy, herbivores only get about 1,000, and carnivores only about 100. This is why there are many more plants than herbivores, and far fewer top predators!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Flexibility in your thinking helps you handle change effectively.

choices.label: D. Energy in a food chain flows in a circle — decomposers give energy back to producers so it goes around forever
choices.feedback: Tricky question! 💡 NUTRIENTS cycle (like carbon and nitrogen going around and around), but ENERGY does not cycle — it flows in ONE direction and is eventually lost as heat. New energy must constantly enter the ecosystem from the sun. Decomposers recycle NUTRIENTS (like nitrogen and phosphorus) back to the soil for plants, but they do not recycle the energy. That is an important difference!

skill_explanation.empathy: Valuing others' experiences alongside your own shows empathetic thinking.

rounds.situation: Dr. Leaf presents shocking statistics: 'Earth is losing species 1,000 times faster than the natural rate. This loss of biodiversity weakens every ecosystem on the planet.' She asks the class to measure biodiversity right here on school grounds using the Shannon Diversity Index — a real scientific formula used by ecologists worldwide. Sam is thrilled about the math. Anika is worried about what they will find.
rounds.goal: Measure and understand biodiversity and learn why diversity makes ecosystems stronger.
rounds.coaching_moment: Ethical reasoning: Biodiversity is not just about counting species — it is about the health and resilience of the living world. Every extinction is an irreversible loss.
rounds.reflection_prompt: If one species of beetle goes extinct, why should we care? How might it affect the whole ecosystem?
rounds.image_prompt: Students counting different species in a quadrat on the school grounds, clipboard with data table, diverse insects and plants visible, scientific fieldwork

choices.label: A. Pollution is only harmful to animals; plants are not affected because they do not breathe or drink water
choices.feedback: Plants are definitely affected by pollution! 💡 Plants DO absorb water through their roots and exchange gases through their leaves. Acid rain damages plant leaves and changes soil chemistry. Oil spills smother roots. Air pollution blocks sunlight needed for photosynthesis. Water pollution kills aquatic plants. When plants die from pollution, all the animals that depend on them are affected too!

skill_explanation.resilience: Staying focused under pressure builds your ability to bounce back.

choices.label: B. Building more roads and houses is always good for ecosystems because animals can use the spaces between buildings
choices.feedback: Urbanization is actually one of the biggest threats to ecosystems! 💡 When we build roads and houses, we fragment natural habitats — breaking them into small, disconnected pieces. Many animals need large, continuous areas to find food and mates. Roads cause roadkill and block animal migration. While a few species (like pigeons and rats) adapt to cities, most wild species cannot survive in urban spaces!

skill_explanation.empathy: Considering how others feel shows emotional intelligence.

choices.label: C. Deforestation, pollution, and urbanization are major human activities that destroy habitats and reduce biodiversity in ecosystems
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Humans impact ecosystems in many ways: deforestation removes animal homes and destroys food webs, pollution poisons water and soil, and urbanization replaces natural habitats with buildings and roads. These activities have caused species to go extinct 1,000 times faster than the natural rate! Understanding our impact is the first step to fixing it.

skill_explanation.ethical_reasoning: Standing by your values even under pressure builds integrity.

choices.label: D. Humans only affect ecosystems near cities; forests and oceans far from people are completely unaffected
choices.feedback: Human impact reaches everywhere! 💡 Even remote ecosystems are affected. Plastic waste has been found in the deepest ocean trenches. Air pollution causes acid rain in distant forests. Climate change from burning fossil fuels is melting polar ice caps thousands of miles from any city. Microplastics have been found in Arctic snow and on Mount Everest. No ecosystem on Earth is untouched by human activity!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Adjusting your approach when conditions change shows flexibility.

rounds.situation: Dr. Leaf takes the class to a nearby vacant lot that was once a thriving meadow before being cleared for construction that never happened. 'This is what human impact looks like,' she says quietly. The bare soil is eroding, there are no birds, and plastic trash litters the ground. 'But the good news? Ecosystems can recover if we help them.' She challenges the class to study human impact AND begin restoration.
rounds.goal: Assess human impact on a degraded ecosystem and propose restoration strategies.
rounds.coaching_moment: Empathy: Understanding how our actions affect other living things is the foundation of environmental responsibility. We share this planet.
rounds.reflection_prompt: What daily actions of yours (positive or negative) affect the ecosystems around you?
rounds.image_prompt: Students examining a degraded vacant lot with eroded soil and trash, contrasted with a nearby healthy green area, clipboards and sampling equipment, thoughtful expressions

choices.label: A. Conservation means keeping only the most popular or beautiful animals safe and letting others go extinct naturally
choices.feedback: Conservation protects ALL species and habitats! 💡 Every species plays a role in its ecosystem, whether it is beautiful or not. Ugly species like vultures clean up dead animals and prevent disease. Earthworms aerate soil for plants. Mosquitoes are food for fish and bats. Conservation means protecting entire ecosystems, not just picking favorites. Even the species we find unappealing have critical roles!

skill_explanation.empathy: Taking others' perspectives into account builds empathy.

choices.label: B. Biodiversity does not matter as long as the largest animals in the ecosystem are healthy
choices.feedback: Every species matters! 💡 Large animals often depend on hundreds of smaller species. Tigers need deer, deer need grass, grass needs soil bacteria, and bacteria need fungi. If we only protected big animals while losing insects, worms, and microorganisms, the entire ecosystem would collapse. Tiny organisms like bees pollinate 75% of our food crops — their loss would be catastrophic!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Being open to new information and changing course builds adaptability.

choices.label: C. It is okay if some species go extinct because new species will evolve quickly to replace them
choices.feedback: Evolution takes millions of years — we cannot wait! 💡 While new species do evolve through natural selection, it takes thousands to millions of years. Humans are causing extinctions 1,000 times faster than new species can evolve. Once a species is gone, its unique genes, adaptations, and ecological role are lost forever. We are losing species faster than nature can replace them!

skill_explanation.resilience: Facing challenges head-on strengthens your resilience over time.

choices.label: D. Biodiversity means the variety of different species in an ecosystem, and higher biodiversity makes ecosystems more stable and resilient
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Biodiversity is like a safety net for ecosystems. With many different species, if one species declines, others can fill similar roles. A forest with 500 species of insects is more resilient than one with just 50 — if a disease kills one species, the ecosystem can still function. Tropical rainforests have the highest biodiversity and are some of Earth's most stable ecosystems!

skill_explanation.ethical_reasoning: Thinking about what's fair for everyone involved shows ethical awareness.

rounds.situation: CRISIS! When you arrive at the pond study zone on Monday morning, the water is cloudy and has a strange chemical smell. Dead fish float on the surface. Fern discovers that a cleaning chemical was accidentally dumped into the school's storm drain, which flows into the pond. Dr. Leaf is devastated: 'This is a real pollution event. Our entire pond ecosystem is at risk. We need to act fast — but carefully.' The Conservation Day showcase is only two weeks away!
rounds.goal: Respond to a pollution emergency and develop a recovery plan for the ecosystem.
rounds.coaching_moment: Resilience: Environmental disasters test everything you have learned. True ecologists stay calm, use their knowledge, and never give up on an ecosystem.
rounds.reflection_prompt: How does one careless action (dumping chemicals) affect an entire ecosystem? What does this teach us about responsibility?
rounds.image_prompt: School pond with cloudy discolored water, dead fish floating, concerned students and teacher in rubber gloves testing water, warning signs posted, tense atmosphere

choices.label: A. Plants do not play any role in the water cycle because they only need water to drink, just like animals
choices.feedback: Plants are major players in the water cycle! 💡 Plants absorb water through their roots and release water vapor through tiny pores in their leaves called stomata — this process is called transpiration. A single large tree can release 100+ liters of water into the air per day! Forests create so much transpiration that they actually generate their own rainfall. Removing forests disrupts the water cycle in the entire region!

skill_explanation.empathy: Understanding the impact on people around you shows care for others.

choices.label: B. The water cycle only happens in oceans; freshwater ecosystems like ponds and rivers get their water from underground springs only
choices.feedback: The water cycle happens everywhere! 💡 Evaporation occurs from ALL water surfaces — oceans, lakes, rivers, puddles, and even soil. Plants release water vapor through transpiration from their leaves. This water vapor rises, condenses into clouds, and falls as precipitation that feeds freshwater ecosystems. Rivers, ponds, and groundwater are all part of one connected global water cycle!

skill_explanation.resilience: Pushing through difficulty builds mental strength.

choices.label: C. Water in ecosystems is used up by animals when they drink it, so rain must create brand new water to replace what was consumed
choices.feedback: Water is never used up or created! 💡 The Earth has had roughly the same amount of water for billions of years. When animals drink water, it eventually returns to the environment through breathing, sweating, and waste. The water you drink today might have been part of a dinosaur's lake millions of years ago! The water cycle continuously recycles the same water through evaporation, condensation, and precipitation.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Pivoting your strategy when needed is a sign of adaptive thinking.

choices.label: D. The water cycle in an ecosystem involves evaporation (liquid to gas), condensation (gas to liquid), precipitation (rain/snow), and collection in rivers and groundwater
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ The water cycle is essential for ecosystems. Water evaporates from oceans, lakes, and rivers into the atmosphere. It condenses into clouds, falls as precipitation (rain, snow, or hail), and collects in rivers, lakes, and underground aquifers. Plants absorb water through roots and release it through leaves (transpiration), contributing to the cycle. Ecosystems cannot survive without this continuous water recycling!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

rounds.situation: One week before Conservation Day! Dr. Leaf gives the teams full creative freedom: 'Design and begin implementing your best conservation project. Use everything you have learned this semester. Think big, but start locally. The best projects create lasting change.' The school grounds are your canvas. Fern says: 'Remember — the best conservation projects benefit both nature AND people.'
rounds.goal: Design and begin implementing an impactful conservation project for the school ecosystem.
rounds.coaching_moment: Creativity: The best conservation solutions combine scientific knowledge with creative thinking. Nature does not need our pity — it needs our ingenuity.
rounds.reflection_prompt: What is the one conservation action that would have the biggest positive impact on your school ecosystem? Why?
rounds.image_prompt: Students working on various conservation projects — planting native species, building bird boxes, installing rain garden, creating wildlife corridors, active and excited

choices.label: A. Soil nutrients never run out because the sun provides all the energy and minerals that plants need
choices.feedback: The sun provides energy, not minerals! 💡 Plants need the sun for photosynthesis (making glucose from CO2 and water), but they also need minerals like nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium from the soil. These nutrients CAN run out if decomposers do not recycle them from dead material. This is why farmers add fertilizer and why composting is so important — it returns nutrients to the soil!

skill_explanation.empathy: Listening to different viewpoints strengthens your empathy skills.

choices.label: B. Soil is just made of tiny rocks and dirt — there are no living things in soil
choices.feedback: Soil is one of Earth's most alive environments! 💡 A single gram of soil can contain up to 10 billion bacteria, plus fungi, tiny worms (nematodes), insects, and earthworms. These organisms are essential — they break down dead material into nutrients, create air pockets for roots, and fight plant diseases. Healthy soil is 50% mineral, 25% air, 20% water, and 5% organic matter and living organisms!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Responding to unexpected situations with creativity shows adaptability.

choices.label: C. Soil is a living ecosystem containing billions of organisms per handful — including bacteria, fungi, earthworms, and insects that decompose organic matter and recycle nutrients for plants
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Soil is incredibly alive! One teaspoon of healthy soil contains more microorganisms than there are people on Earth. These tiny decomposers break down dead leaves, animal waste, and dead organisms into nutrients like nitrogen and phosphorus that plants need to grow. Earthworms create tunnels that let air and water reach plant roots. Without soil organisms, plants could not grow and ecosystems would collapse!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: D. Earthworms are harmful to soil because they eat plant roots and create holes that let water drain away too fast
choices.feedback: Earthworms are soil heroes! 💡 Earthworms are incredibly beneficial. They eat dead plant material (not living roots) and their waste (called castings) is rich fertilizer. Their tunnels actually HELP the soil by allowing air and water to reach plant roots, preventing waterlogging. Charles Darwin called earthworms 'the most important creatures on Earth.' A healthy garden can have over 1 million earthworms per acre!

skill_explanation.resilience: Choosing to persist when things get hard develops resilience.

rounds.situation: Conservation Day is here! The school grounds are buzzing with visitors — parents, teachers, younger students, and a reporter from the local newspaper. Your ecology projects are displayed and your restored habitats are open for tours. Dr. Leaf says: 'This is your moment. Show the world what you have learned and why ecosystems matter.' How will you present your work?
rounds.goal: Present your ecology knowledge and conservation work at the showcase.
rounds.coaching_moment: Resilience: Sharing your work publicly takes courage. Whether you win an award or not, inspiring others to care about nature is the real victory.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Looking back at Week 1, how has your understanding of ecosystems changed? What was the most surprising thing you learned?
rounds.image_prompt: School Conservation Day event, students presenting ecology projects to visitors, nature displays, posters about food webs, restored pond area, proud moments, outdoor setting

choices.label: A. Every species in an ecosystem is equally important, so there is no such thing as a keystone species
choices.feedback: While all species have value, some have disproportionate impacts! 💡 Research shows that certain species affect their ecosystems far more than others relative to their numbers. When these 'keystone species' are removed, the entire community changes dramatically. When wolves returned to Yellowstone, they changed deer behavior so much that rivers actually shifted course because vegetation grew back on riverbanks! Not all species have such powerful effects.

skill_explanation.resilience: Learning from setbacks rather than giving up shows resilience.

choices.label: B. If a keystone species goes extinct, the ecosystem will quickly produce a new keystone species to take its place
choices.feedback: Ecosystems cannot quickly replace keystone species! 💡 When a keystone species disappears, the ecosystem often suffers a 'trophic cascade' — a chain reaction of changes through multiple levels of the food web. It can take decades or centuries for an ecosystem to find a new balance, and sometimes it never fully recovers. This is why conserving keystone species is a top priority for ecologists!

skill_explanation.empathy: Valuing others' experiences alongside your own shows empathetic thinking.

choices.label: C. A keystone species is always the largest, most dominant animal in the ecosystem, like a lion or elephant
choices.feedback: Keystone species are not always the biggest! 💡 A keystone species is defined by its outsized IMPACT on the ecosystem, not its physical size. Bees are tiny but are keystone pollinators — without them, most flowering plants cannot reproduce, which affects all animals that eat those plants. Sea stars, prairie dogs, and even some fungi are keystone species. Impact matters more than size!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Flexibility in your thinking helps you handle change effectively.

choices.label: D. A keystone species is one that has a very large effect on its ecosystem relative to its population size — removing it causes the whole ecosystem to change dramatically
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Keystone species hold an ecosystem together like a keystone holds an arch. Sea otters are a classic example — they eat sea urchins, which eat kelp forests. When otters were hunted nearly to extinction, sea urchins exploded in number and destroyed vast kelp forests, which were home to hundreds of other species. One small species can make or break an entire ecosystem!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.
skill_explanation.ethical_reasoning: Choosing what's right over what's easy shows moral courage.

glossary_terms.definition: A community of living organisms (plants, animals, microbes) interacting with each other and their non-living environment (air, water, soil, sunlight).
A linear sequence showing how energy and nutrients pass from one organism to another. Each arrow means 'is eaten by'. Example: Grass → Rabbit → Fox.
A complex network of interconnected food chains in an ecosystem, showing all the feeding relationships. More realistic than a single food chain.
An organism (usually a plant) that makes its own food from sunlight through photosynthesis. Producers form the base of every food chain.
An organism that gets energy by eating other organisms. Primary consumers eat plants (herbivores), secondary consumers eat herbivores (carnivores).
An organism (like fungi, bacteria, or earthworms) that breaks down dead matter and returns nutrients to the soil, completing the nutrient cycle.
The variety of different species living in an ecosystem. Higher biodiversity generally means a healthier, more resilient ecosystem.
The natural environment where an organism lives, which provides the food, water, shelter, and conditions it needs to survive.
A feature (structural, behavioral, or physiological) that helps an organism survive and reproduce in its specific environment. Example: a camel's hump stores fat for desert survival.
A non-native organism introduced to an ecosystem where it has no natural predators, allowing it to spread rapidly and harm native species.
A diagram showing that energy decreases at each trophic level. Only about 10% of energy passes from one level to the next.
A species that has a disproportionately large effect on its ecosystem relative to its abundance. Removing a keystone species can cause the ecosystem to collapse.

endings.title: Ecosystem Master
endings.message: You have achieved mastery in the Ecosystem Explorer program! Your ecology knowledge is extraordinary, your conservation efforts have transformed the school grounds, and your field skills rival those of professional ecologists. Dr. Leaf nominates you for the Junior Ecologist Award, and the newspaper features your conservation projects on the front page. You have proven that understanding nature is the first step to protecting it!

endings.title: Skilled Ecologist
endings.message: You have become a skilled ecologist with solid knowledge and good field practices! Your Conservation Day presentation demonstrates real understanding of ecosystems and biodiversity. Dr. Leaf says you are ready for the advanced environmental science elective next year. Your future in ecology is bright!

endings.title: Nature Explorer
endings.message: You completed the Ecosystem Explorer program with a growing appreciation for nature. Some weeks were challenging, but you stuck with it and learned the basics of ecology and conservation. Dr. Leaf says there is always next semester to go deeper. Keep exploring — every great ecologist started as a curious beginner!

endings.title: Struggling Explorer
endings.message: The Ecosystem Explorer was a tough journey for you. Many of the ecological concepts were confusing, and fieldwork did not always go as planned. But you did not give up. Dr. Leaf arranges extra tutoring and says: 'Nature rewards patience. The students who struggle most often develop the deepest respect for how complex and wonderful ecosystems really are.' Your story is just beginning!

endings.title: Ecosystem Under Threat
endings.message: The school ecosystems have suffered significant damage this semester. Biodiversity has dropped, the pond is still recovering, and many species have left. It is a hard lesson, but Dr. Leaf reminds you: 'Even the most damaged ecosystems can recover if we give them the right care. What matters now is learning from these mistakes and trying again next semester.' Fern has already started planning the recovery.
